findings.claim: The period is called the Personal Rule, not the 'Eleven Years' Tyranny' — that label was Whig propaganda used by his opponents.
findings.truth: 'Eleven Years' Tyranny' is a label from later Whig historians hostile to Charles, not a term used by his contemporaries or opponents, and it is still used in textbooks. Declaring one term correct and the other wrong teaches a false rule.
findings.evidence: standard historiography of the Personal Rule (Gardiner and later Whig writers coined the phrase)

findings.claim: Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, was impeached and executed in May 1641.
findings.truth: Strafford was impeached in November 1640, but the impeachment collapsed. Parliament condemned him by an Act of Attainder, which Charles signed on 10 May 1641; Strafford was executed on 12 May 1641. Lesson 2 of this unit already states the attainder correctly.
findings.evidence: standard record of Strafford's trial; unit L2 content_html

findings.claim: examiners reward candidates who link financial and religious grievances to the specific Scottish crisis
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: William Prynne, Henry Burton and John Bastwick were imprisoned and had their ears cut off in 1637.
findings.truth: Burton and Bastwick lost their ears in 1637. Prynne had already lost his in 1634 for Histriomastix; in 1637 the stumps were cropped and he was branded. The simplification is standard at GCSE, so no edit.
findings.evidence: standard record of the 1637 Star Chamber punishments

findings.claim: Examiners reward correct enumeration — learn all five. (data-revision-tip on the Five Members key fact)
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Examiners want to see you explain why each event made civil war more likely, not just describe what happened.
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners want. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Charles reportedly said: 'I see the birds have flown.'
findings.truth: The words are reported in several forms ('all my birds have flown', 'I see the birds are flown'). The version used is a normal rendering, so no edit.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Five Members' (Field 2011: 'all my birds have flown')

findings.claim: The First Civil War (1642-1646) killed an estimated 85,000 in combat and around 100,000 civilians through disease and dislocation — perhaps 4% of England's population.
findings.truth: Those figures cover the whole of England's civil wars, August 1642 to September 1651, not the First Civil War alone: about 84,830 combat deaths (34,130 Parliamentarian, 50,700 Royalist) and roughly 100,000-127,000 non-combat deaths, of which around 40,000 were civilians. The deaths were mostly from disease, not all civilian.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'English Civil War' casualty table (Clodfelter); Carlton's ~3.7% of population figure

findings.claim: His disciplined cavalry — which he called 'Ironsides'
findings.truth: Cromwell did not coin the name. Prince Rupert is said to have called Cromwell 'Old Ironsides' after Marston Moor, and the nickname then passed to his troopers.
findings.evidence: standard account of the Ironsides nickname

findings.claim: in late 1644 Parliament passed the Self-Denying Ordinance
findings.truth: The Commons first passed a self-denying ordinance in December 1644 but the Lords rejected it. The Self-Denying Ordinance became law on 3 April 1645. The lesson's own glossary and definition already say April 1645, so the sentence contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: standard record; unit L3 glossary_terms and dfn data-def

findings.claim: examiners reward analysis of turning points rather than a chronological list of battles
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: It was also notably religioniously heterodox
findings.truth: 'religioniously' is not a word, and the sentence is unreadable as printed.
findings.evidence: plain-language rule

findings.claim: In April 1645 Parliament established the New Model Army.
findings.truth: The New Model Ordinance passed the Lords on 15 February 1645; the army was mustered and took the field in the spring. 'April 1645' is a defensible date for when it was in being, so no edit.
findings.evidence: standard record of the New Model Ordinance

findings.claim: Some (e.g. Sean Kelsey) argue Charles stage-managed the trial as a propaganda victory for royalism, knowing his refusal to plead would undermine the court's legitimacy.
findings.truth: That is not Kelsey's argument. Kelsey argues the court hoped the trial would force Charles into a settlement, and that the death sentence was not a foregone conclusion; it was Charles's refusal to plead that closed off the alternative. Attributing the reverse case to a named living historian is a misattribution.
findings.evidence: Kelsey, 'The Trial of Charles I' (EHR 2003) and 'Politics and Procedure in the Trial of Charles I'

findings.claim: Royalist resistance in Ireland led by the Catholic Confederacy
findings.truth: By 1649 the Irish war was run by the Royalist Marquess of Ormond in alliance with the Confederate Catholics, whose own association had been folded into that alliance. The shorthand is loose but not wrong enough to edit.
findings.evidence: standard record of the second Ormond Peace, January 1649

findings.claim: At Wexford the following month, a similar number were killed [i.e. about 3,500], including many civilians.
findings.truth: Between 1,500 and 2,000 soldiers and civilians died in the sack of Wexford on 11 October 1649, over 300 of them drowning in the river. The Drogheda figure of about 3,500 is roughly twice the Wexford toll.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Sack of Wexford': 'between 1,500 and 2,000 soldiers and civilians died'

findings.claim: Match question pairs Drogheda with 'October 1649 — Irish campaign'.
findings.truth: Drogheda was stormed on 11 September 1649; Wexford was the October siege. The lesson's own text says September 1649, so the answer key marks the true answer wrong.
findings.evidence: unit L6 content_html and flashcards; standard record of the Drogheda siege

findings.claim: It had sat for thirteen years
findings.truth: The Long Parliament first met on 3 November 1640 and Cromwell dissolved the Rump on 20 April 1653 — twelve years and five months.
findings.evidence: standard dates of the Long Parliament and the dissolution of the Rump

findings.claim: Examiners expect candidates to explain Cromwell's reasons, not just describe what he did.
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners expect. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Parliaments were to meet every three years, with a minimum of 160 days.
findings.truth: The Instrument of Government required a Parliament at least once every three years and forbade dissolving one within the first five months of its sitting. There is no 160-day rule, and the next sentence of the same lesson calls it 'the minimum five-month period'.
findings.evidence: Instrument of Government articles VII-VIII; unit L7 content_html next sentence

findings.claim: the 'regicides' — the men who had signed Charles I's death warrant. Thirteen were executed
findings.truth: Thirteen men were executed for the regicide (ten in 1660, three in 1662), but only nine of them had signed the death warrant. The others ran the trial or the execution: John Cook prosecuted, Hugh Peters preached, Daniel Axtell commanded the guard, Francis Hacker signed the order to the executioner. The definition given makes the figure of thirteen wrong.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Regicide': six warrant signatories executed in 1660 plus Okey, Barkstead and Corbet in 1662

findings.claim: examiners reward students who know its specific content and that all promises were deferred to Parliament
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: the castle was held for Parliament under Sir Edward Peyto, a local Parliamentarian gentleman who had been its constable [Kenilworth, from 1642]
findings.truth: Sir Edward Peyto held WARWICK Castle for Parliament, not Kenilworth. Kenilworth was used by Charles I as a base for Midlands raids on his advance to Edgehill in October 1642; after the battle the Royalist garrison withdrew as Lord Brooke approached and Parliament garrisoned it. The governor named in the record is Hastings Ingram, arrested in April 1643 as a suspected Royalist double agent.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle' (Hughes, Politics, Society and Civil War in Warwickshire); English Heritage Kenilworth history page

findings.claim: In 1644 Royalist forces made a brief assault on the castle but failed to take it.
findings.truth: No Royalist assault on Kenilworth in 1644 is recorded. What is recorded is that by January 1645 the Parliamentary forces at Coventry had strengthened their hold on the castle and Royalist attempts to dislodge them from Warwickshire failed. The castle saw no major fighting.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle' (Hutton); English Heritage: 'no major combat'

findings.claim: the ruined state of Leicester's Gatehouse and the great hall are all products of 1649-50
findings.truth: Leicester's Gatehouse is not ruined. Colonel Joseph Hawkesworth, who carried out the slighting, converted it into his own house; it stayed the principal dwelling on the site and is the best-preserved building at Kenilworth today. A student describing the physical evidence would be marked wrong.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle' (Morris 2010, p.50-51); English Heritage Kenilworth history page

findings.claim: Hyde did not restore the castle — it remained largely ruined — but built a new house using stone from the castle.
findings.truth: No new Hyde house is recorded. The ruined castle continued to be worked as a farm with Leicester's Gatehouse as the principal dwelling; the remaining buildings were stripped for their materials, and the King's Gate was added to the outer bailey wall for farm workers.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle' (Morris 2010, p.51)

findings.claim: Charles II granted the Kenilworth estate to Sir Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, in 1661.
findings.truth: 1661 is too early. English Heritage dates the grant to 1665. Wikipedia has the Queen Mother Henrietta Maria holding the castle first and the grant following her death. Either way the estate was not granted in 1661, the year Hyde received his earldom.
findings.evidence: English Heritage Kenilworth history page ('In 1665, King Charles II granted Kenilworth to ... Hyde'); Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle'

findings.claim: The process at Kenilworth included the deliberate demolition of the great walls of the keep (the Norman tower), the removal of the roof of the great hall and other internal buildings, and the draining of the mere.
findings.truth: One wall of the great tower was destroyed, not 'the great walls'. The documented slighting also breached the outer bailey wall and the battlements — the north side of the outer bailey wall was almost entirely destroyed — and the remaining buildings were stripped for materials rather than simply unroofed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle' (Pettifer p.258; Morris 2010 p.50); English Heritage: 'destroying the north wall of the keep and breaching the outer curtain wall'

findings.claim: Practice set labelled '2 marks — Describe One Feature', '4 marks — Describe Two Features' and two '5 marks — Historic Environment Explain'.
findings.truth: The historic environment is examined in Section B by two questions only: an Explain question worth 10 and a source comparison worth 10. There is no 2, 4, 5 or 16 mark form. Labels relabelled and the Describe stems rewritten as Explain stems.
findings.evidence: spec, British depth study with historic environment assessment table (Component group 3): Section A Q1 Explain 10, Q2 essay using sources 20 + 5 SPaG (35 marks, 45 min); Section B Q1 Explain 10, Q2 source comparison 10 (20 marks, 30 min); paper 55 marks, 1 hr 15.

findings.claim: Royal proclamations 'were printed by the Stationers' Company and distributed to sheriffs across the country', repeated in the glossary, a dfn definition, a fill knowledge check and a practice mark scheme.
findings.truth: Royal proclamations were printed by the King's Printer, who held the royal patent for statutes, proclamations, Bibles and prayer books; the Stationers' Company was the book trade's guild and licensing body. I could not find a source that states this plainly enough to correct it under the brief's rule, and the fix ripples through five fields including a fill question whose only answer is 'Stationers''. OPTIONS: (a) replace 'Stationers' Company' with 'King's Printer' in the content, the dfn, the glossary and the practice scheme, and re-cut the fill question so it tests the sheriffs' role instead; (b) drop the printer entirely and say the proclamations were printed under royal licence and sent to sheriffs to be read out, re-cutting the same fill question; (c) leave as is. Recommendation: (a).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Robert Barker (printer)': 'Much of his printing work was of an official nature, including prayer books, scriptures, and law books'
findings.ruling: King's Printer in body, tooltip, glossary, conclusion; fill question re-cut to sheriffs.

findings.truth: This depth study is examined in Section A by two questions only: an Explain question worth 10 and an essay using sources worth 20 plus 5 for spelling, punctuation and grammar. summary: Every lesson carried a practice set labelled in another board's forms and tariffs (2/4/8/16 mark Describe, Explain Causation and Significance labels, plus 5-mark historic environment labels); all ten sets are relabelled to the paper's real forms - Explain 10 and essay using sources 20 + 5 SPaG in Section A, Explain 10 and source comparison 10 in Section B. The serious content errors are all in the Kenilworth site lesson: Sir Edward Peyto held Warwick Castle, not Kenilworth; the 1644 Royalist assault on the castle is not in the record; Leicester's Gatehouse is the one building the slighting spared, not a ruin it created; and the Hyde grant is dated 1665, not 1661. Elsewhere: the Wexford death toll was doubled (1,500-2,000, not a second 3,500), a match question dated Drogheda to October 1649 against the lesson's own September, the First Civil War carried the casualty figures for all three wars, the Self-Denying Ordinance was dated to late 1644 against its own glossary, and the Instrument of Government gained a 160-day rule it never had. Six fabricated examiner claims removed. Lesson 4 was clean apart from the practice labels.
